summary: Describes a signed XML data format, the Validation Token, with which validation entities can securely say that a telephone number was validated for an ENUM domain registration. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Before you get an internet name tied to a phone number, someone checks it. The token is a signed paper that proves the check was done.

questions: how to prove enum number ownership
what is an enum validation token
how is an enum validation token signed
what is a validation entity in enum
how long is an enum validation token valid
subtitle: A signed XML token a validation entity hands to an ENUM registry to prove a phone number was checked.

tldr.problem: An ENUM domain name is tied to an E.164 phone number, so the registry needs trustworthy proof that the registrant is the number's assignee before it delegates the domain.
tldr.mechanism: A Validation Entity issues a Validation Token, an XML document with the number, the entity, the registrar, the method and dates, an optional block of holder data, and an enveloped XML-DSIG signature.
tldr.outcome: The registry can check who validated what, for which registrar and until when, and can reject forged, altered or replayed tokens. The token is signed but not encrypted.

today: RFC 5105 is a Proposed Standard from December 2007, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sits in the ENUM validation family alongside RFC 4725 and RFC 5076.

sections.title: Why a Validation Token
sections.content:
An ENUM domain name (RFC 3761) that corresponds to an existing E.164 phone number may only be delegated with the authorization of that number's Assignee. In the role model of RFC 4725, the party that performs this check is the Validation Entity (VE). Checking that the Registrant is the Assignee is commonly called validation.

By sending a Validation Token, a signed XML document, to the Registry, the VE certifies that the delegation requirements have been met and are current. The RFC also notes that the idea may suit other registries where proof of an underlying right is a condition of registration, such as a top level domain with a sunrise phase, or a number portability database.
sections.eli5: A checker looks at your phone number and signs a note saying it is yours. The note goes to the place that hands out the internet name.

sections.title: What the Token Must Carry
sections.content:
In this model the token is the only data passed from the VE to the Registry, so it must hold everything the Registry needs under its policy. The Registry needs confirmation that the token came from an accredited VE, that its duration of validity conforms to policy, that the validation met minimum requirements, and that it is protected against tampering and replay attacks.

The token may also carry number holder information, which can make a later revalidation simpler. For example, if the first validation checked both the Registrant's identity and the number's ownership, a revalidation only needs to re-check ownership. XML is used because tokens will travel inside XML-based Registry/Registrar protocols such as EPP (RFC 4930).
sections.eli5: The note has to say who checked, how, and for how long it is good, and it has to be impossible to fake or reuse.

sections.title: The Digital Signature
sections.content:
The link between Registry and VE is assumed to be untrusted. A Registrar may carry the token along with the request, for instance, and has no role in asserting the right to use the number. So the token carries a digital signature that gives authenticity (the indicated VE made it), integrity (no tampering in transit) and non-repudiation (the validation can be audited).

The signature follows XML-DSIG (RFC 3275). Exclusive XML canonicalization MUST be used, so namespace declarations inherited from a surrounding document do not break the signature. The signature is enveloped, making it part of the token, and it covers all information in the token.

A VE MUST be able to sign per XML-DSIG, MUST support RSA-SHA1 and RSA-SHA256 (RFC 4051), MUST support RSA key sizes of 1024 and 2048 bits, and MUST be able to embed X.509 certificates. The RFC says that advances in cryptanalysis cast doubt on SHA1, which makes XML-DSIG's SHA1 recommendation obsolete. The Registry MUST define in local policy which algorithms and key sizes it accepts. A public key infrastructure is not required: whether the Registry acts as certification authority, accepts certificates from a public one, or only uses pre-registered keys is local policy.
sections.eli5: The checker puts a special seal on the note. If anyone changes a single word, the seal breaks, and the seal can only come from the real checker.

sections.title: The validation Element
sections.content:
Every token MUST contain a <validation> element. Its parts are:

  • a serial attribute, unique per VE;
  • one <E164Number> in fully qualified international format, and an optional <lastE164Number> that extends the validation to a whole block of numbers (both numbers MUST be the same length);
  • <validationEntityID>, <registrarID> and <methodID>, naming the VE, the Registrar the validation was done for, and the method used;
  • <executionDate>, the validation date as an RFC 3339 full-date;
  • an optional <expirationDate>. The Registry revokes the delegation on that date unless a new token extends it, and a missing date means infinite validity.

The format and uniqueness rules of the IDs are left to the Registry's local policy, so they need no IANA registration.
sections.eli5: This is the main part of the note: which number, who checked, for which shop, how they checked, when, and when the check runs out.

sections.title: Optional Holder Data
sections.content:
A token may contain a <tokendata> section about the number holder. It holds a <contact> with the organization, a <commercialregisternumber> (the company's official registration number, interpreted per country), title, first name, last name, and an <address> with street name, house number, postal code, locality, county, state or province, and an ISO country code.

There can be up to 10 <phone>, 10 <fax> and 10 <email> elements, with phone and fax as full E.164 numbers. Everything directly under <tokendata> is optional. The country uses the alpha-2 code from ISO 3166-1, and the first five address elements follow E.115 Computerized Directory Assistance version 2.
sections.eli5: The note can also list the owner's name, address and phone numbers, which saves time when the check has to be repeated.

sections.title: Example Tokens
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples. The first is an unsigned token with no holder data, for the number +442079460200 through +442079460499, showing the basic layout. The second is a signed token for +442079460123 with a <tokendata> section and an X.509-based RSA-SHA256 signature that embeds the signer's certificate, so the signature can be verified without a key server.

The RFC adds that a valid signature is necessary but not sufficient. Anyone evaluating a token must also check other factors, such as the certificate and the XML schema.
sections.eli5: Two sample notes show how it looks: a bare one, and a fully sealed one with the owner's details.

sections.title: Formal Syntax and Registrations
sections.content:
Two XML schemas define the token. The token core schema covers the mandatory parts: a token element with a required Id attribute, a validation element, an optional tokendata element and a required XML-DSIG signature. E.164 numbers are limited to 20 characters and the ID fields to 1 to 20 characters. The token data schema defines the tokendata section, with most text fields limited to 256 characters.

IANA registered four URNs for the two namespaces and two schemas, including urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:enum-token-1.0 and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:enum-tokendata-1.0.
sections.eli5: The schemas are the strict form that says which boxes the note must have and how long each answer may be.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The token is only as secure as the XML-DSIG algorithms under it. A generic signature check is not enough. The Registry must also confirm that the signature uses approved transforms and algorithms, that it references the <token> element, and that the key belongs to an accredited VE. The signature points at the token through Id="TOKEN", and moving that attribute to another element such as <tokendata> would make the signature worthless.

The token is not encrypted, so confidentiality needs a different mechanism. The Registry MUST verify that the token matches the delegation request and that the expiration date, including the absence of one, fits its policy. The <registrarID> stops a second Registrar from using an eavesdropped token. To block replay, local policy MUST say how long after <executionDate> a token can authorize a delegation.
sections.eli5: A good seal is not enough. The receiver must check that the seal covers the whole note, comes from a trusted checker, and that the note is not too old or meant for a different shop.
